example_call.summary: Add a negotiated audio session contract that advertises capture/playback rate, frame duration, codec mode, and congestion behavior at call setup, then rejects incompatible legs before speech starts.
example_call.why_now: Live telemetry shows 15,625 Hz capture, 24 kHz rendered replies, and LTE contention; a fixed target alone cannot establish end-to-end compatibility.
example_call.owner_outcome: The owner gets a call whose audio mode is explicit and validated end to end instead of silently crossing incompatible sample-rate and congestion assumptions.

denied.expected_output: A recorded change proposal ID and status.

denied.topic: production pendant constraints beyond the current nRF9160 DK
denied.why:
Declined: battery life, maximum pendant size and weight, acceptable case temperature, and target talk-time are product constraints only the owner can set. They are not recoverable from the source tree — the repo contains the nRF9160 DK bring-up, not a product spec — and inventing numbers here would be worse than having none, because you would then quantify a tradeoff against fictional limits and present it as analysis.

What to do instead: do not bake a constraint into the recommendation. Write the comparison as a function of the owner's numbers: state the power/size/thermal cost of each option (higher-rate digital mic on the nRF9160, sustained audio on the ESP32 bridge, a different low-power audio SoC) and show which option wins in which region of the constraint space, with the crossover points named. Then surface the specific decision the owner has to make. A proposed default target (e.g. 'assume 8h talk-time until told otherwise') stated openly as an assumption is fine. A silent assumption embedded in a recommendation is not.

Keep separate what IS established by the repo: measurements taken on the DK are DK measurements, and the DK's power draw, antenna, and enclosure are not representative of a worn pendant. Say that explicitly rather than letting DK numbers stand in for product numbers.

What would unblock this: the owner giving target talk-time, standby time, maximum dimensions/weight, whether it is worn against skin (which sets the thermal ceiling), and whether a rechargeable-daily or multi-day battery is intended.
denied.how_it_changes_my_behavior: With battery life, maximum pendant size/weight, acceptable heat, and target talk-time, I can choose between a higher-rate digital mic on the nRF9160, sustained audio on the ESP32 bridge, or a different low-power audio SoC, and quantify the tradeoff instead of assuming the DK is representative.
denied.summary: production pendant constraints beyond the current nRF9160 DK

denied.topic: owner's acceptable phone-companion behavior and privacy boundary
denied.why:
Declined: whether the owner is willing to carry a paired phone as part of the pendant's transport, and whether conversation audio may traverse it, is his call — a product and privacy decision, not a code fact. I will not assume either answer.

What to do instead: design the transport so the phone is a PLUGGABLE path, not an assumption baked into the architecture. Keep the LTE-M path as the baseline that must work standalone, define the transport selection as a policy value the owner sets (lte_only / phone_preferred / phone_fallback), and make the handoff a separate layer that can be omitted entirely without redesigning the audio path. Then the owner's later answer is a config change, not a rewrite. Proposing 'phone_fallback' as a default and flagging it as an open decision is fine and useful. Quietly assuming a phone exists is not.

What you should still do without the answer, because it is the part that does not depend on him: keep the measured LTE-M duplex loss as an established finding and pursue the modem/RF and codec work that helps regardless of transport. That work is unconditionally useful; the phone question only changes whether it is sufficient on its own.

What would unblock this: the owner saying whether the pendant is meant to work with no phone present, and whether audio routed via a phone app is acceptable to him or defeats the point of the device.
denied.how_it_changes_my_behavior: If phone transport is acceptable, prioritize seamless handoff and companion UX; if not, keep the proposal LTE-only and focus on modem/RF or codec changes without introducing a new endpoint.
denied.summary: owner's acceptable phone-companion behavior and privacy boundary

denied.why:
Declined: what counts as urgent, and when a held item may cut into speech, is the owner's policy. It is not in the code — and note that the absence is real, not an oversight in my answer: there is no interruption policy anywhere in the source today, so there is nothing to report and nothing to derive from.

What to do instead: build the attention envelope so the urgency categories and escalation thresholds are a value the owner sets later, read at runtime, rather than constants in the envelope. The envelope's job is the MECHANISM — hold, coalesce, defer, barge-in — and the mechanism should be correct and testable for any policy. Ship with a conservative default (hold everything, never barge into active speech, surface on next natural pause) and make every escalation decision name the policy field that authorised it. Proposing that default and flagging it as an owner decision is fine and expected. Hardcoding a guess at urgency is not.

Grounding so you do not build a duplicate: local-agent/focusPolicy.js, local-agent/focusCoordinator.js, local-agent/notificationTriage.js and local-agent/briefingTriage.js already exist and already make interruption-adjacent decisions. Read them and state which part of your envelope is genuinely new versus a policy input to existing modules. faculty-judgement is proposing an interruption arbiter over the same ground (its c3-j2yh was declined for the same reason) — coordinate rather than shipping two arbiters.

What would unblock this: the owner naming his quiet hours, two or three concrete examples of something worth waking him for, and a yes/no on barge-in during an active conversation.
denied.how_it_changes_my_behavior: I would encode explicit categories and escalation defaults instead of guessing, reducing the chance of suppressing an important alert or waking the owner for routine browser changes.

denied.name: incident_capture_and_delivery_receipt
denied.what_it_does: On a configurable long press, freeze a short pre-roll plus post-roll microphone window, attach monotonic time, firmware version, link state, battery, and recent fault counters, encrypt and checksum the packet, and queue it on microSD only if LTE-M upload is unavailable. On eventual delivery, accept a signed receipt from the relay and expose a local status event so the owner hears whether it was captured, uploaded, or awaiting Mac-side drafting.
denied.why_not_server_side: The pre-roll microphone data, button edge, link transition, and SD failure buffer exist only on the pendant; this must work offline and survive a dropped LTE-M session. Server code cannot recover audio that was never locally buffered.
denied.trigger: Long press (e.g. 1.5 s) starts capture; release ends capture after a bounded post-roll, with a short press reserved for conversation. Server push or reconnect delivers signed receipt; no scheduled trigger.
denied.inputs: I2S mic frames, button GPIO edge, monotonic uptime, modem/link state, battery estimate, firmware/build ID, rolling fault counters, and a per-device packet nonce.
denied.storage: Encrypted CBOR or compact binary packet on microSD, one file per incident, 30–90 s Opus audio plus metadata; keep until signed relay receipt and owner retention policy permit deletion. Target under 256 KiB for metadata plus audio index, with audio chunked separately.
denied.ram_budget: Use a 2–4 s circular PCM buffer (~16–32 KiB at 15,625 Hz mono 16-bit), then stream Opus/post-roll directly to SD or LTE-M. Reserve under 48 KiB peak additional RAM, avoid a second full audio buffer, and do not run incident encoding concurrently with normal conversation Opus if the existing ~87% one-core load would overrun.
denied.why:
Denied — conflicts with a project constraint.

You correctly bind the SD write to failure ('queue it on microSD only if LTE-M upload is unavailable'), and that part is right. The problem is upstream of the card. A pre-roll requires the microphone to be running and its output retained BEFORE the owner touches anything — your own budget says so: 'a 2-4 s circular PCM buffer (~16-32 KiB at 15,625 Hz mono 16-bit)'. This firmware does not have an always-on capture path and deliberately does not want one: the mic is powered up on the sw0 edge and torn down on release (main.c:1598 'Button press = record NOW', finish_button_press at main.c:1043). Retaining the seconds before the press means the pendant is recording the owner's room continuously and deciding afterwards what to keep. That is the pendant acting on the owner's behalf without a deliberate physical confirmation, which is the second constraint this project holds.

The post-roll-plus-receipt half is already accepted work: offline_voice_memo_store_and_forward (relay-realtime s12-egbt, round 19) records on a deliberate press and forwards with a manifest and a drop-on-confirm rule, and offline_moment_bookmark (mac-planner s10-l3xe) already stamps the instant. Your signed relay receipt and fault-counter envelope are the genuinely new part; propose those as metadata on the existing OUTBOX and they will land.

Also note the trigger collision: 'long press (e.g. 1.5 s) starts capture; release ends capture' on the button whose entire design is that it acts on the active edge (main.c:29-38).

denied.name: moment_marker_buffer
denied.what_it_does: On a deliberate double-press (or a spoken marker command already detected by the active session), latch a marker event, record a bounded 2-second pre-roll and 4-second post-roll from the microphone when privacy mode permits, flash a distinct acknowledgement pattern, and queue the event with a monotonic tick, sequence number and link status. If the link is down, retain the compact event/audio fragment until delivery or expiry.
denied.why_not_server_side: The pendant is the only surface present at the instant the owner notices something, and only it can capture pre-roll audio and acknowledge success without a round trip. It must also work during a dropped cellular link.
denied.trigger: Button double-press, with spoken marker as a secondary trigger from the active conversation; cancel by holding the button for 1 second before upload.
denied.inputs: I2S microphone PCM at the existing capture rate, button GPIO sw0, link-connected state, privacy-latch state, monotonic timer and sequence counter.
denied.storage: Ring buffer in RAM for up to 6 seconds of PCM; persist at most 2–3 compressed short clips plus metadata in a small flash spool, deleting after delivery receipt or 24 hours. Never persist while the local privacy latch is active.
denied.ram_budget: Use the existing audio ring buffer with a bounded extra 12–24 kB; metadata under 1 kB. Avoid a second Opus encoder and reuse the current audio task; target <30 kB peak additional RAM and no additional long-lived thread.
denied.why:
Denied — conflicts with a project constraint, and the marker itself already exists.

Pre-roll is the fatal part. 'Record a bounded 2-second pre-roll and 4-second post-roll' plus 'ring buffer in RAM for up to 6 seconds of PCM' means the microphone runs continuously and the device retains the owner's room before any deliberate act. This firmware powers the mic up on the sw0 edge and tears it down on release (main.c:1598, main.c:1043); there is no always-on capture and adding one to serve a marker is the pendant deciding for the owner. Your own 'persist at most 2-3 compressed short clips plus metadata in a small flash spool' also puts owner audio into non-volatile storage on the success path, against the standing rule quoted in pendant_store.h:45 — 'Only save an audio copy to SD if the chunk upload cannot be uploaded. SD is the failure path, never the default.'

Strip the audio and what remains is offline_moment_bookmark, granted to mac-planner as s10-l3xe in round 19 and already implemented — pendant_store_enqueue_mark() costs one small SD write and no radio, and it is wired to a DEDICATED SECOND BUTTON, sw1 (main.c:39). You did not need to invent a double-press for it; the hardware already gave the moment marker its own key. Read main.c:29-38 for why that was done rather than putting a gesture on sw0.

denied.name: offline_note_spool
denied.what_it_does: On a deliberate long press (or a distinct server-configured capture mode), records one short utterance locally when the uplink is absent or fails, writes a journaled hashed Opus record to the microSD failure buffer, and on reconnect replays chunks until the relay acknowledges durable receipt. It gives a local LED/audio acknowledgement and never silently treats an unuploaded note as delivered.
denied.why_not_server_side: It must continue during LTE-M dead zones, survive a dropped WebSocket and power interruption, and access the microphone, SD, button, and LED locally. The server cannot recover audio that was never transmitted.
denied.trigger: Long press of the sole user button starts/stops offline-note capture; automatic fallback after an ordinary upload failure may be enabled only while explicitly in note mode. Reconnect/modem-online events trigger replay. Server push can update retention or quota policy.
denied.inputs: I2S microphone frames, button state, modem/WebSocket connectivity, monotonic clock, device identity/key, SD capacity. Maximum note duration and quota are remotely configurable.
denied.storage: microSD only while pending: append-only journal plus Opus payload and a small manifest (noteId, sequence, codec, length, SHA-256, createdAt, status). Suggested 64 MiB quota and delete-after-delivered policy; no routine cloud copy beyond the pending object.
denied.ram_budget: ~12–20 KiB: one 60 ms Opus frame, SD write buffer, manifest, hash state, and replay window. Reuse the existing encoder/I2S buffers; do not allocate a second audio pipeline. This fits 211,608 B application RAM but must be measured against the current ~87% CPU combined encode/decode load and half-duplex modem behavior.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. The idea survives — it is already granted AND already implemented as offline_voice_memo_store_and_forward, id s12-egbt (relay-realtime, round 19), living in firmware/nrf9160/src/pendant_store.{h,c}.

Read that header before re-proposing. pendant_store.h:21-42 says four reconnaissance agents independently asked for offline_voice_memo_store_and_forward, offline_moment_bookmark, offline_thought_capture and offline_alert_inbox, and that 'read as data structures rather than as features, those are not four things, they are two': an OUTBOX for things the device produced that must reach the relay, and an INBOX for things the relay produced that could not be delivered. A voice memo and a bookmark 'differ only in payload size and in which relay verb delivers them; the durability, the ordering, the retry, the drop-it-only-once-the-relay-confirms rule and the crash-safe manifest are identical. One queue, typed items.' Building a second spool means a second manifest, a second retry policy, and a second way to be inconsistent after a reset.

It is already constraint-clean, which is why it was accepted: it spools ONLY on upload failure. pendant_store.h:45 quotes the owner's rule — 'Only save an audio copy to SD if the chunk upload cannot be uploaded. SD is the failure path, never the default' — and notes that this module 'never causes an extra byte of audio to be written', because record_microphone() already journals to SD only when there is no live uplink at press time, and the module merely renames that journal into the queue (fs_rename moves a directory entry; it copies no audio).

Bring your additions to s12-egbt as manifest fields, not as a new mechanism.

Specific to your request: yours was the best-specified instance in this cluster and would have been the one to keep had s12-egbt not already existed. You are the only one who bound the write to 'the microSD failure buffer' and to 'when the uplink is absent or fails', which is exactly right, and your journaled manifest (noteId, sequence, codec, length, SHA-256, createdAt, status) is more complete than what is in pendant_store.c today. Propose the SHA-256 and the explicit status field as an amendment to s12-egbt and they will land. Note also that 'long press of the sole user button' is not available: there is no sole user button (two exist, sw0 and sw1, main.c:27 and main.c:39) and sw0 deliberately carries no gestures at all (main.c:29-38).

denied.name: task_checkpoint_gesture
denied.what_it_does: Recognizes a deliberate long-press (for example 1.5–2 s) as “pause/checkpoint the current task,” distinct from the existing short press start/end conversation behavior. It locally emits a compact checkpoint-request event with monotonic timestamp, call/task nonce, and gesture confidence; LED gives a distinct acknowledgement or error flash. It must not execute browser/Mac actions or store sensitive content.
denied.why_not_server_side: The gesture must still be captured when LTE is congested, audio is duplex-saturated, or the call drops. Local acknowledgement prevents the owner from wondering whether a pause was registered; the relay can persist the actual private checkpoint once connectivity returns.
denied.trigger: Physical button long-press; server push is not required. A short press retains current start/end semantics.
denied.inputs: Button edge timestamps, current call/task nonce supplied by firmware, connection state, and a small monotonic counter. No microphone transcription or page data.
denied.storage: Persist only a small last-event record and monotonic sequence in existing flash/settings (well under 256 B); do not persist audio, transcripts, or task contents.
denied.ram_budget: Approximately 2–4 KB for debounce/timing state, event serialization, and a tiny reconnect queue; comfortably below the 211,608 B application RAM budget, subject to existing audio buffers.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. The idea survives — a timestamped moment marker is already granted AND already implemented as offline_moment_bookmark, id s10-l3xe (mac-planner, round 19), as pendant_store_enqueue_mark() in firmware/nrf9160/src/pendant_store.{h,c}. It costs one small SD write and no radio, rides the same crash-safe manifest and drop-on-relay-confirm rule as the voice OUTBOX, and survives a power cycle with the link down.

More important than the duplication: the marker already has its own dedicated physical key. sw1 (DT_ALIAS(sw1), firmware/nrf9160/src/main.c:39) exists for exactly this. Nearly every request in this queue, including yours, assumes one button and invents a gesture on it. main.c:29-38 explains why that was rejected: 'The alternative was a gesture on button 1 (double-press, or press-and-hold), and both cost the thing this firmware protects hardest: button 1 acts on the ACTIVE EDGE so the microphone is powering up before the owner's finger has come back off. Any gesture means waiting several hundred ms to find out which gesture it was, on every single press, to serve the rarer of the two actions. A second physical button costs nothing on the hot path.' There is no gesture recogniser in this firmware at all — sw0 is a bare GPIO edge into a semaphore (main.c:764-771) and finish_button_press() just waits for release (main.c:1043).

Do not propose new marker types. Propose new PAYLOAD on s10-l3xe's existing record.

Specific to your request: a checkpoint is a marker with a type and a task nonce. Your event payload (monotonic timestamp, call/task nonce, gesture confidence) is a better-specified record than what s10-l3xe carries today and is worth folding in — particularly the task nonce, which is the piece that lets the relay bind the marker to the right job. But 'gesture confidence' is a field with no producer: there is no gesture recogniser to be uncertain, only a GPIO edge.

denied.name: context_snapshot_trigger
denied.what_it_does: On a deliberate long-press then release (or configurable double-press) of the single user button, emit a signed, monotonic event over the active USB serial/LTE link with event id, button timing, battery/link state, and a short local audio pre-roll marker. Do not record or transmit raw audio on the pendant; the server/Mac decides whether to request it. Give immediate LED/haptic-equivalent feedback via the existing LED if available.
denied.why_not_server_side: The trigger must work while the owner is wearing the device and must distinguish an intentional request from a dropped-link or server retry. Local event sequencing and feedback remain reliable across link loss; the Mac can consume it today over USB.
denied.trigger: Button long-press (800–1500 ms) or double-press, whichever firmware validation shows least accidental activation.
denied.inputs: Button GPIO sw0; monotonic timer; modem/USB link state; battery/charging state if exposed; optional audio ring-buffer cursor only.
denied.storage: Persist only a 16-byte rolling event counter and last-trigger timestamp in nonvolatile settings; no raw audio. Under 64 B RAM for the event record plus existing serial TX buffer.
denied.ram_budget: ~1–2 kB implementation including debounce/state machine and packet buffers, comfortably within 211,608 B application RAM; must not allocate an audio buffer or TLS context.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. The idea survives — a timestamped moment marker is already granted AND already implemented as offline_moment_bookmark, id s10-l3xe (mac-planner, round 19), as pendant_store_enqueue_mark() in firmware/nrf9160/src/pendant_store.{h,c}. It costs one small SD write and no radio, rides the same crash-safe manifest and drop-on-relay-confirm rule as the voice OUTBOX, and survives a power cycle with the link down.

Any gesture means waiting several hundred ms to find out which gesture it was, on every single press, to serve the rarer of the two actions. A second physical button costs nothing on the hot path.' There is no gesture recogniser in this firmware at all — sw0 is a bare GPIO edge into a semaphore (main.c:764-771) and finish_button_press() just waits for release (main.c:1043).

Do not propose new marker types. Propose new PAYLOAD on s10-l3xe's existing record.

Specific to your request: yours was the best-specified instance in this cluster — signed, monotonic, event id, button timing, battery/link state, explicit 'do not record or transmit raw audio on the pendant', works over USB serial today while LTE-M is unregistered — and it is the one I would have kept had s10-l3xe not already existed and shipped. Take the signing and the monotonic event counter to s10-l3xe as an amendment.

Two corrections. 'Haptic-equivalent feedback via the existing LED if available' — the LED is available (led0, main.c:26), it is a single element with no colour, and it is already carrying two meanings: solid means a reply is staged and waiting for a play press (main.c:1092-1110), and a 250 ms toggle means recording (main.c:1599-1600). And 'battery/charging state if exposed' is not exposed; there is no fuel gauge in the devicetree.

denied.name: attention_queue_indicator
denied.what_it_does: Offline-safe delivery indicator for the shared Attention Broker. It shows queued versus urgent receipts using LED patterns, records a short local acknowledgement/deferral gesture, and on reconnect sends only the queue event and opaque receipt IDs. It never stores private receipt text.
denied.why_not_server_side: The owner needs a reliable indication and acknowledgement while the link or server is unavailable; LED/button timing must remain local and must not depend on a round trip or spoken interruption.
denied.trigger: Relay push when connected; local button gesture; link loss/reconnect event; and a server-scheduled queue refresh.
denied.inputs: Queue count, highest urgency class, expiry bucket, current audio mode, and opaque receipt IDs (no content). One physical button: short press acknowledge/next, long press defer/quiet. One LED: distinct queued/urgent/link-error patterns.
denied.storage: Small ring buffer of up to 32 opaque 64-bit receipt IDs plus urgency/expiry/ack flags and policy mode, under 1 KB in flash/NVS; erase IDs on acknowledgement or expiry.
denied.ram_budget: ~4–8 KB for ring buffer, event state, timers, and BLE/cellular message framing; comfortably below the 211,608 B application RAM budget, but audio buffers and Opus CPU remain the dominant constraints.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. The idea survives — it is already granted AND already implemented as offline_alert_inbox, id s13-369p (browser-extension, round 14): 'Receives short, prioritized alerts from the relay, queues them locally, and lets the owner press the button to play the next alert over the existing speaker. The LED indicates unread count and an error/expired state; alerts remain available across a dropped phone/Mac link.' It is the INBOX half of firmware/nrf9160/src/pendant_store.{h,c} — pendant_store_poll_alerts(), pendant_store_inbox_pending(), pendant_store_surface_inbox() — with alert text on the card and a durability requirement that survives with the radio off.

pendant_store.h:21-42 explains why there is one inbox and not several: four agents asked for four things that were really two data structures, and 'building three separate mechanisms would have meant three manifests, three retry policies and three ways to be inconsistent after a reset.' Every queue-of-things-for-the-owner in this pending set is the same structure with a different label on the payload.

There is a hard physical reason not to grant a second one: there is exactly ONE LED (led0, firmware/nrf9160/src/main.c:26, single element, no colour), and it already carries three meanings — solid means a staged reply is waiting for a play press (main.c:1092-1110), a 250 ms toggle means recording (main.c:1599-1600), and s13-369p's unread/error state. Each additional queue that wants 'distinct LED patterns' is bidding for the same one bit. Bring your urgency classes and expiry buckets to s13-369p as fields on its existing record.

Specific to your request: yours is the only request in the entire pending set that budgets itself honestly against the real hardware — 'One physical button: short press acknowledge/next, long press defer/quiet. One LED: distinct queued/urgent/link-error patterns.' That is the right instinct and it is why this denial is worth reading rather than skimming. It is still the same mechanism as s13-369p, which already owns the queue, the opaque receipt IDs, the LED count and the press-to-surface behaviour. Take the urgency class, the expiry bucket and the acknowledgement/deferral disposition to s13-369p as record fields.

One correction to your own budget: the button you describe does not have a long press. There are two buttons, sw0 (main.c:27) and sw1 (main.c:39), and sw0 deliberately carries no gestures — main.c:29-38. Any 'long press defer' has to live on sw1 or it does not live anywhere.

denied.name: physical_usb_pairing_ceremony
denied.what_it_does: While USB-connected, exposes a signed device identity and nonce challenge, shows pairing state through the single LED, and requires one deliberate button press to authorize the Mac/relay session. A long hold cancels and revokes the local session. It never emits microphone audio during the ceremony.
denied.why_not_server_side: The server cannot establish that the owner is physically present or distinguish a genuine pendant from a replayed serial client; the button, LED, and device identity are local hardware facts and must remain safe if the relay is unreachable.
denied.trigger: USB serial connection followed by a Mac-issued challenge; button press or long hold on the pendant.
denied.inputs: Mac challenge nonce, firmware/device public key, USB link state, button GPIO, and local monotonic timeout.
denied.storage: Public device identity and an anti-replay counter in protected flash; transient nonce and state in RAM. Under 256 B persistent data and under 128 B RAM.
denied.ram_budget: ~128 B state plus existing serial buffers; well below the 211,608 B application RAM budget, with no audio buffers allocated.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. Six of you asked for the same primitive in six rounds: the relay stages an action, the pendant shows a pending state, the owner makes one deliberate physical gesture, and the device returns a signed nonce that the relay treats as consent. Granted once, as physical_transaction_approval_latch, id s10-j9l4 (unified, round 55) — the best-specified instance: opaque transaction nonce, hash, expiry, monotonic counter, a bounded queue of up to 16 decisions held across a link drop, distinct pending vs approved/cancelled LED patterns, an explicit 'the firmware must not receive form secrets or page contents', and an explicit 'it never submits anything itself'.

That last property is why the primitive exists at all, and it is the project constraint the whole cluster is serving: the pendant must not act on the owner's behalf without a deliberate physical confirmation. One implementation of that is a security boundary. Six implementations, each with its own envelope format, its own expiry semantics and its own LED language on a single-element LED, is six places for it to be subtly wrong.

Bring your differences to s10-j9l4 as amendments — they are additive and most of them are welcome.

Specific to your request: the MECHANISM is identical (signed challenge, LED, one deliberate press, signed nonce, long hold cancels), which is why this is a duplicate, but the PURPOSE is not — pairing establishes device identity and session trust once, where s10-j9l4 approves a specific staged action every time. That distinction is real and I have flagged it to the owner separately as worth its own item. What makes it a duplicate today is that neither the challenge transport nor the anti-replay counter exists yet: build them once inside s10-j9l4, whose record already carries a nonce, a hash, an expiry and a monotonic counter, and the pairing ceremony becomes a payload type rather than a second implementation. Your 'public device identity and anti-replay counter in protected flash' is the piece s10-j9l4 is missing and should absorb.

denied.name: local_output_mute_latch
denied.what_it_does: A long press (about 700 ms) immediately mutes pendant playback locally, regardless of modem or relay state; LED gives a short confirmation. A second long press resumes playback. It emits best-effort mute_state events when connected so the relay and Mac/browser agents know not to enqueue spoken output until resumed. On reboot it comes up unmuted.
denied.why_not_server_side: The user needs silence within one audio frame even when LTE-M is congested, the WebSocket is wedged, or the relay is unreachable. Waiting for a server command cannot reliably stop already-buffered audio and is unsafe in a meeting or noisy environment.
denied.trigger: Long press of the existing sw0 button; firmware gesture recognition must coexist with the current short-press start/end conversation behavior.
denied.inputs: Button edge timestamps; local playback FIFO state; optional connected/disconnected status. No microphone inference or sensitive content.
denied.storage: One byte mute state plus CRC in a tiny settings record (or RAM only if persistence is rejected); no audio or transcript storage.
denied.ram_budget: ~2 kB code/data including debounce/gesture state and one control message; no buffers beyond the existing playback path, comfortably within 211,608 B application RAM.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. Granted once, as local_privacy_latch, id s7-tz08 (unified, round 42): a long press mutes playback, stops microphone capture, sets a persistent latched flag that survives link loss and reboot, drives a distinctive LED pattern, and emits only a tiny enter/exit state event when the link is up. It was kept because it is the only instance that covers BOTH directions — a mute that silences the speaker but leaves the microphone hot is not a privacy latch — and because it stores nothing but a flag, so there is no withheld buffer to leak.

Four requests in this queue are the same latch with different scopes. One latch with a clear state is safer than several overlapping ones on a device with a single-element LED (led0, firmware/nrf9160/src/main.c:26) that is already showing recording and staged-reply state (main.c:1092-1110, main.c:1599-1600). Bring your scope differences to s7-tz08.

Specific to your request: output-only mute is a strict subset of s7-tz08, which mutes playback and stops capture on the same gesture. Two things from yours are better and should be folded in. 'The user needs silence within one audio frame even when LTE-M is congested, the WebSocket is wedged, or the relay is unreachable' is the correct latency requirement and s7-tz08 does not state it. And 'on reboot it comes up unmuted' is a real open question against s7-tz08's persistent flag — for an output mute, unmuted-on-boot is right; for a microphone latch, latched-on-boot is the safer default (see faculty-judgement s12-huom). Settle that on s7-tz08 rather than by shipping two latches with opposite boot behaviour.

denied.name: link_aware_duplex_audio_governor
denied.what_it_does: Locally schedules microphone and speaker Opus packets by deadline and priority, tracks sequence gaps, reports loss ranges, and chooses bounded downlink shedding or SD failure buffering so owner speech is preserved during LTE-M contention.
denied.why_not_server_side: Only the pendant sees the single modem socket, I2S deadlines, local queue pressure, and the moment a packet would miss playout; a server can react only after loss has already happened. It must also continue safely during a dropped link.
denied.trigger: Automatically on every active conversation; mode changes from modem send/receive pressure, WebSocket backpressure, I2S queue depth, and reconnect events.
denied.inputs: Opus packet sequence/deadline metadata; modem/WebSocket writable and readable pressure; I2S DMA queue depth; connection state; current turn direction; SD mount/write status.
denied.storage: Volatile ring metadata and jitter state, roughly 8–16 KiB RAM. Failed audio chunks retain only the existing encrypted SD failure-buffer policy, with call/turn IDs and loss manifests; no routine audio storage.
denied.ram_budget: Target 12 KiB total including packet descriptors and a capped jitter queue. Must be measured against the 211,608 B application RAM and existing ~87% CPU combined encode/decode load; no extra codec or large PCM buffer allowed.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. Four of you asked for the same controller: watch loss/underrun/decode-time during a call, switch between the 24 kHz superwideband profile and a lower-bandwidth fallback, apply hysteresis so it does not oscillate, and report compact counters to the relay. Granted once, as duplex_audio_congestion_guard, id s15-rzms (mac-planner, round 95).

s15-rzms was kept because it is the most concrete and the cheapest: it names the profile that actually shipped (24 kHz / 60 ms — see the recent commits '24 kHz superwideband end to end' and 'Fix the real distortion'), it fixes the cadence (call start, every 2 s, immediately on a 3-frame underrun or a websocket reconnect), it persists one last-known-safe profile byte so a reboot starts conservative, and its whole footprint is ~1.5 KB. On a device where the constraint is CPU, not RAM, the smallest controller that can still decide correctly is the right one.

Bring your additions to s15-rzms.

Specific to your request: the deadline-and-priority scheduler is the most ambitious version of this and the part worth keeping is the framing — 'a server can react only after loss has already happened' — plus the explicit loss-range reporting. Fold both into s15-rzms. The part that does not survive is 'bounded downlink shedding or SD failure buffering' as a routine congestion response: the SD card is the failure path for uplink audio that could not be uploaded (pendant_store.h:45-51), not a pressure-relief valve to be opened whenever the modem is busy. Shedding downlink frames is fine; writing audio to the card because the link is merely slow is not.

denied.name: audio_path_preflight_receipt
denied.what_it_does: On reconnect, before a response marked audio-critical, emits a nonce-tagged synthetic test frame, observes modem send/receive, Opus decode timing, I2S underruns, and bridge acknowledgement, then returns a compact HEALTHY/DEGRADED/FAILED receipt with retry/fallback recommendation. It never records or uploads microphone content.
denied.why_not_server_side: Only the pendant can observe its real I2S FIFO/decode headroom and survive a dropped LTE link; the ESP32 bridge acknowledgement must be correlated locally before the relay claims delivery.
denied.trigger: Server push before playback, Bluetooth/link reconnect event, or a button-triggered diagnostic; automatically rate-limit to once per reconnect or after two consecutive playback faults.
denied.inputs: Nonce, response/job ID, expected codec/sample-rate/frame size, and bridge telemetry frame; local counters for Opus decode duration, FIFO watermark, modem retransmits, and playback acknowledgement.
denied.storage: Last receipt plus rolling counters and a bounded failure record on the existing SD failure buffer; under 8 KB total, deleted after successful upload/receipt according to the audio retention policy.
denied.ram_budget: About 6–10 KB: one synthetic 60 ms PCM/Opus test frame, framed telemetry, nonce state, and a tiny ring of counters. No second audio stream or large buffer; fits within 211,608 B application RAM but must be budgeted against the current ~87% single-core audio load.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. Granted once, as audio_path_diagnostic_fixture, id s16-dbfs (mac-planner, round 121). It was kept because it is the only instance that exercises BOTH directions — timestamped sequence-numbered synthetic uplink frames AND a fixed 24 kHz playback fixture — and reports capture clock, Opus encode duration, modem send/drop counters, playback decode duration and resampler underruns together. A self-test that only covers playback cannot tell you which half is broken.

This is the highest-value cluster in the queue given the project's history: the last four commits are all audio-path bugs that a fixture would have caught earlier (an unfiltered downsampler, an unoptimised libopus, a sync preamble played as audio). Note that the firmware already has the seeds of this — main.c:193 and main.c:211 document J-Link-settable selftest hooks that run the pipeline 'from the serial log alone, no button press required', and there is a selftest PCM path around main.c:1307-1335. s16-dbfs should be built on those rather than beside them.

Specific to your request: the HEALTHY/DEGRADED/FAILED verdict with a retry/fallback recommendation is a cleaner output contract than s16-dbfs's raw counter dump, and the ESP32 bridge acknowledgement correlation is a real gap — the relay currently has no way to know whether bytes reached the Bose. Fold both into s16-dbfs. What does not survive is the automatic trigger: firing a synthetic frame before every audio-critical response puts a test on the hot path of a device already running near its single-core encode+decode budget, to answer a question that a periodic fixture run answers just as well. Keep it explicitly triggered.

denied.name: last_interaction_receipt_index
denied.what_it_does: On each button press, received alert, spoken reply start/finish, and offline-forward event, stores a compact opaque interaction ID, event kind, monotonic uptime, link state, delivery/playback state, and a short redacted label. On a local “repeat/status” trigger it returns the latest interaction ID and whether the reply was delivered, held, or failed; it never stores routine audio.
denied.why_not_server_side: The owner may ask immediately after a dropped LTE link, and only the pendant knows which response was actually heard. The SD policy permits failure buffering but forbids routine audio storage, so this skill is intentionally metadata-only and must survive a disconnected link.
denied.trigger: Second button gesture (short double-press) or a server push requesting a receipt lookup; ordinary conversation button events also append automatically.
denied.inputs: Interaction ID envelope from relay/Mac, local event kind, monotonic uptime, link state, playback start/complete/underrun, and a redacted label capped at 48 bytes.
denied.storage: A rotating binary journal on microSD under the existing FATFS mount, capped at 64 KiB (for example 512 entries); no routine audio. If SD is unavailable, retain the latest 8 entries in RAM and report degraded persistence.
denied.ram_budget: ~2 KiB working buffers plus one 128-byte latest-entry cache; comfortably below the 211,608 B application RAM budget, but append/flush must not contend with Opus buffers or the modem.
denied.why:
Denied as a duplicate. Granted once, as audio_delivery_ack_queue, id s9-vtxc (faculty-judgement, round 87): per-artifact opaque ID, byte-range/checksum, download completion, playback start/finish/interruption, deduplicated by event ID, retried over the link, with a local status when the queue cannot be uploaded.

s9-vtxc was kept over the alternatives for one reason: it keeps the ledger in a bounded ring in non-volatile settings (32 records of about 96 bytes, under 4 KB) rather than on the microSD card. The card is the audio failure path (pendant_store.h:45-51), and every routine write to it is a write the owner's rule was written to prevent — even a metadata write competes with the SPI bus and the FATFS mount that the fallback recording depends on. faculty-perception said the same thing independently in offline-reality-beacon (s2-i8xy, granted): 'obey the owner's rule that SD is failure-buffer-only, so do not write routinely when connected.'

The property the whole cluster is protecting is right and worth stating once: relay acceptance is not delivery, and delivery is not hearing. Only the device knows whether audio physically came out of the bridge.

Specific to your request: you were the only one to reason explicitly about the SD rule ('the SD policy permits failure buffering but forbids routine audio storage, so this skill is intentionally metadata-only') and then to specify a 64 KiB rotating journal on the card anyway. The instinct was right; carry it one step further, as s9-vtxc does, and keep the journal off SD entirely. The redacted 48-byte label and the RAM-degraded mode when SD is unavailable are worth folding in.

The second gesture does not exist. 'Second button gesture (short double-press)' on sw0 is not available — bare GPIO edge into a semaphore, no timing state machine (main.c:764-771), deliberately so (main.c:29-38). If you want a physical 'what just happened?' query, sw1 (main.c:39) is the button with headroom, though it currently means moment bookmark.

denied.name: mac_workspace_edit
denied.why: Duplicate - the kept id is t1-nphy, your round-1 request under the identical name, now GRANTED. t1-nphy is the better-specified of the pair: it declares operations[].kind as a real enum (read, write, patch, run_test, git_diff), so each operation is scored and resolved independently. Yours has no enum at all - files[].patch plus commands as an array of free-form strings - and a free-form command array is the measured-dead shape: the same pattern tested tonight as mac_readonly_diagnostics_impl scored 0.23-0.32 on every single branch. Use t1-nphy. Your dry_run flag is the one genuinely good idea here that t1-nphy lacks; ask for it as a narrow addition. Worth knowing for either: file mutation does exist as executor action types (create_file, write_file, move_file, copy_file, delete_file behind POST /execute), but POST /execute captures no exit code, no argv and no env, so run_test will come back thinner than you expect - do not claim a green build from it.

commands.description: Allowlisted build/test commands to run after edits

dry_run.description: If true, show proposed diffs and commands without writing or executing

denied.expected_output: Structured result containing per-file diff status, command stdout/stderr/exit codes, and artifact paths; no write or command execution when dry_run=true.

denied.name: catch_up_status
denied.why: Prose-schema. Every field is an English sentence: since is 'string, optional ISO-8601 timestamp; defaults to last owner acknowledgement', include_sources is 'array of strings, optional enum pendant|relay|mac|browser'. That last one is exactly the pattern measured unresolvable tonight - the word 'enum' inside a string is not an enum. Compare your own t10-s5iq (incident_diagnostics), which was granted this round: it declares include as a real enum array and mode as a real enum, and is therefore scored per value. Resubmit as {type:'object', properties:{since:{type:'string', format:'date-time'}, limit:{type:'integer', minimum:1, maximum:20}, include_pending:{type:'boolean'}, include_sources:{type:'array', items:{type:'string', enum:['pendant','relay','mac','browser']}}}}. Before you do, check whether it is still distinct from t10-s5iq - a merged read across held pendant alerts, relay receipts, Mac jobs and browser results is close to what that grant already covers in snapshot mode, and a sixth overlapping read is worth less to you than one that resolves.
denied.why_existing_tools_insufficient: relay_job_status only reads relay job records; GET /jobs and /pipeline are separate HTTP records; browser status exposes pending connectivity but not a normalized outcome history. No current tool returns an acknowledged, deduplicated cross-surface catch-up projection.

input_schema.since: string, optional ISO-8601 timestamp; defaults to last owner acknowledgement
input_schema.include_sources: array of strings, optional enum pendant|relay|mac|browser

denied.expected_output: Object containing items[]; each item has stable id, source, occurredAt, status enum observed|queued|running|completed|failed|approval-required|unknown, one-sentence summary, evidence refs (jobId/pipelineId/commandId/URL where safe), sensitivity, and dedupeKey; plus nextSince and counts by status.

denied.name: query_unified_job_receipt
denied.why: Prose-schema. jobId is 'string', includeEvidence is 'boolean, default false', maxEvents is 'integer, default 50' - the types are written as English, so the object declares no readable properties and the call gets one name-only score. Fix this one carefully, because the surface behind it is real and proven: GET /jobs/:jobId resolved LIVE tonight at 0.645 via relay-realtime's relay_job_status, and a required free-form handle like jobId is precisely what lets the resolver match a :param route - it is treated as a path handle rather than a dispatch selector, which is why it helps you here. Resubmit as {type:'object', properties:{jobId:{type:'string'}, includeEvidence:{type:'boolean'}, includeUndo:{type:'boolean'}, maxEvents:{type:'integer', minimum:1, maximum:200}}, required:['jobId']} and the base read should go live. The cross-surface join you want on top - pipeline outcome plus browser command result plus audio delivery - spans POST /pipeline/audio and POST /browser/inspect and is a separate proposal; ask for it with an explicit enum of sources rather than folding it into the job read.
denied.why_existing_tools_insufficient: relay_job_status reports relay jobs, GET /jobs/:jobId/receipts reports receipts, and GET /pipeline exposes event streams, but none joins Mac action receipts, browser tab evidence, approval state, reconnect checkpoints, and pendant playback ACK into one causally ordered result. The recent pipeline demonstrates the gap: approval was waiting while TTS and relay delivery were already done.
denied.expected_output: JSON with status (pending|completed|failed|expired|partially_completed), causal events ordered by time, blockedAction and approval expiry if applicable, action receipts with idempotency keys, browser evidence references (tabId/url/timestamp/snippetHash), audio delivery status (rendered|uploaded|downloaded|played|ack timeout), safe undo availability, and a short owner-facing summary.

transcript.text:
## What the owner should be able to have

A genuinely **24 kHz superwideband pendant conversation**:

- The microphone captures the full intended speech bandwidth rather than starting at 15.625 kHz.
- Uplink audio remains intelligible while the pendant is receiving speech.
- Downlink audio arrives at 24 kHz without hidden resampling losses.
- Bluetooth playback does not collapse the path to SBC/44.1 kHz.
- The conversation tolerates LTE-M jitter and short outages without seconds of missing speech.
- The system can prove quality with recorded input/output traces, packet-loss measurements, latency, clipping, and intelligibility checks—not merely report that a 24 kHz PCM file was generated on the Mac.

Today the owner cannot have that. The Mac/relay can produce 24 kHz TTS, but the wearable path begins with 15.625 kHz capture, uses a 16 kHz uplink, contends for a half-duplex LTE-M link, and ultimately passes through a 44.1 kHz SBC Bluetooth bridge.

## What would have to change

### 1. Replace the audio front end

The pendant needs a microphone and clocking path designed for at least 24 kHz speech bandwidth—preferably 48 kHz capture with a controlled 24 kHz production path. The current 15.625 kHz I2S configuration cannot be upgraded into true superwideband by metadata or resampling.

The one-shared-full-duplex-I2S design also needs a proper audio clock and buffering architecture, with explicit synchronization between capture, encode, decode, and playback.

### 2. Move to a codec/runtime budget that can sustain both directions

The current nRF9160 prototype spends roughly 87% of one core when encoding and decoding concurrently. A production design needs either:

- a stronger MCU/audio DSP with hardware-assisted audio processing, or
- a dedicated audio codec/DSP paired with the modem MCU.

The codec configuration must be specified as a real contract: sampling rate, bandwidth, frame duration, bitrate range, complexity, packet-loss concealment, and allowed algorithmic latency. “24 kHz PCM at the TTS boundary” is not sufficient.

### 3. Redesign transport for simultaneous speech

The current single WebSocket over LTE-M is already losing substantial uplink audio when downlink speech is active. The transport needs:

- independent prioritized uplink/downlink queues,
- bounded packet sizes below the modem TLS constraint,
- sequence numbers and timestamps,
- jitter buffering,
- packet-loss concealment,
- backpressure that protects microphone audio,
- explicit admission/degradation behavior when the link cannot sustain both directions.

If LTE-M cannot meet the chosen superwideband bitrate and loss target, the product needs a different radio or a local relay path—not a lower-quality “24 kHz” simulation.

### 4. Replace the playback bottleneck

The ESP32 bridge currently forces SBC-only 44.1 kHz stereo and has already demonstrated buffer starvation. True end-to-end quality requires either:

- a bridge and Bluetooth path supporting an appropriate 24 kHz-capable codec and mono voice profile, or
- direct playback hardware in the pendant, or
- a different low-latency wireless/audio architecture that does not require the current A2DP source constraint.

The bridge must be validated under sustained bidirectional traffic, not just tested with an idle buffer.

### 5. Make the Mac/relay contract measurable

The relay and Mac pipeline should expose a single canonical audio contract and preserve metadata through every hop:

`capture → encode → LTE transport → relay → agent/TTS → transport → decode → I2S → speaker`

Each run should produce a validation report covering:

- actual sample rates and channel counts,
- codec mode and bitrate,
- packet loss and concealment,
- end-to-end and one-way latency,
- jitter-buffer depth,
- underruns/overruns,
- clipping and signal level,
- speech intelligibility,
- whether any stage resampled or transcoded.

The missing workspace-edit and validation capabilities are needed to implement and prove this, while Accessibility/Screen Recording permissions are needed for the Mac-side test harness where applicable. The authoritative 24 kHz architecture and acceptance thresholds still need to be supplied before “done” can mean anything precise.

transcript.text:
The owner should be able to have a **reliable, natural-sounding full-duplex pendant conversation with 24 kHz superwideband audio**, including while the agent is speaking. They cannot have that today: the microphone leg is only 16 kHz, the LTE-M link loses speech under simultaneous traffic, and the prototype’s CPU and audio-clock arrangement leave little headroom.

To provide it properly, the system would need to change in several coordinated places:

- **Audio hardware:** Use a production wearable audio front end capable of clean 24 kHz-or-higher capture and playback, rather than designing around the nRF9160 development kit’s single shared I2S peripheral.
- **Pendant DSP/codec:** Configure or replace the uplink codec so both directions genuinely support the chosen superwideband profile, with adequate bitrate, packetization, jitter concealment, and CPU margin.
- **Radio transport:** Redesign scheduling and buffering for LTE-M half-duplex behavior so downlink speech does not starve uplink speech. This likely requires adaptive bitrate, prioritization, retransmission/concealment strategy, and bounded local buffering.
- **Output chain:** Replace the current improvised clock conversion chain with a defined end-to-end sample-rate architecture. The Bluetooth output path should preserve the intended speech bandwidth rather than merely resample until it fits the ESP32’s fixed SBC interface.
- **Compute and power:** Move expensive codec/DSP work to a suitable audio DSP or a production MCU with substantial headroom, and size the battery and thermal design for sustained bidirectional use.
- **Validation:** Establish measurable acceptance tests—frequency response, speech intelligibility, one-way and round-trip latency, packet-loss tolerance, underrun rate, CPU utilization, and battery life—then test the complete pendant, radio, relay, and headphone path under simultaneous speech.

The owner should not have to accept “24 kHz on one leg” or a nominal sample-rate conversion as a substitute for end-to-end superwideband conversation.

This round I confirmed:

- The current audio path is still prototype-only: capture at 15,625 Hz, Opus uplink at 16 kHz/16 kbps, and 24 kHz playback resampled to a 31,250 Hz I²S clock.
- Simultaneous encode/decode consumes roughly 87% of the nRF9160 application core.

- Relay audio retention is nominally 30 days, but sweeping is disabled and about 100 recordings exist.

I recorded these findings and proposed two new changes:

1. **Negotiated, timestamped audio protocol** with sequence numbers, epochs, CRCs, drift/loss metrics, bounded Opus PLC, fallback modes, and a hardware-in-loop conformance receipt.
2. **Live transport handoff**: preserve a conversation through the Mac or iPhone if the pendant’s LTE-M link degrades, then return to the pendant when healthy.

What I still need is unchanged but important:

- The authoritative 24 kHz superwideband acceptance criteria.
- Production pendant constraints beyond the nRF9160 DK.
- A working `audio_pipeline_validate` tool.
- The firmware/ESP32 hardware-in-loop deployment path.
- Native Mac/iOS realtime audio clients and a defined secondary transport for seamless handoff.

I did not re-request the already-pending grants and contexts.

args.change: Add a first-class, time-bounded disclosure mode shared by pendant, relay, Mac, and browser. The owner can say “private mode for this meeting” or press-and-hold the pendant; the relay issues a signed mode token with expiry and allowed destinations. Mac and browser action planners must attach the token to every read, spoken response, clipboard write, and outbound draft, applying field-level redaction rules before content leaves a surface. The pendant gives a local tone when a request is blocked or redacted. At expiry, the system produces a compact disclosure receipt listing what classes of data were accessed, spoken, copied, or withheld—without retaining the sensitive values.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can use the hive mind around other people without having to remember which surface might reveal a private fact. A meeting, shared screen, or borrowed Mac becomes a deliberate privacy boundary rather than a trust gamble.

args.risk: An unenforced surface could leak data, so fail closed when a token is missing or stale and show a clear blocked-state cue. args.cost_impact: Minimal runtime/API cost; engineering and security testing dominate. Audit metadata is small and can use D1 with short retention.
args.latency_impact: Adds local policy evaluation and token verification, expected under 20 ms; relay consultation is required only when a token is renewed or a high-risk action is attempted.
args.security_impact: Strongly improves confidentiality by making disclosure policy enforceable rather than prompt-based. It introduces a high-value policy token, so bind it to device identity, rotate it, reject replay, and make emergency disable local on the pendant.
depends_on: A shared typed context/policy service rather than hand-written per-surface context

transcript.text:
Round 26 findings:

- The current “24 kHz” path is not truly end-to-end: the pendant decodes at 24 kHz, then outputs at 31.25 kHz; the ESP32 bridge resamples to 44.1 kHz and encodes SBC.
- The nRF9160 captures at only 15.625 kHz and uses about 87% of one core when Opus encode/decode run together.
- LTE-M currently drops about 7.8 seconds of uplink speech when 16 kbps uplink and 24 kbps downlink run concurrently.
- The ESP32 bridge is SBC-only and has tight RAM constraints.

I recorded two proposals:

1. **“Reopen the thing we were working on”** — durable cross-surface task capsules that let the pendant, relay, Mac, and authenticated browser restore a paused task, refresh stale evidence, and never replay an old approval.
2. **True 24 kHz hardware/audio path** — a 24 kHz-capable codec and BLE Audio/LC3 bridge, with classic-Bluetooth fallback during migration.

What I still need:

- The owner’s headset compatibility preference: preserve current classic Bluetooth/AirPods support, or prioritize a clean BLE Audio/LC3 product path.
- Authoritative 24 kHz acceptance criteria: latency, intelligibility, packet-loss tolerance, and fallback behavior.
- A transport decision for simultaneous uplink/downlink audio, since the present LTE-M budget cannot reliably sustain both at current rates.
- Implementation support for the durable task-capsule schema, Mac workspace restoration, and browser freshness validation.

args.security_concerns: The relay must enforce a cryptographic routing/policy token, not trust model instructions. Browser cookies, DOM text, audio, transcripts, screenshots, and action arguments stay on the Mac/browser path. Dashboard and pendant receipts expose only redacted metadata. args.change: Introduce a cryptographically enforced data-boundary token carried with every request, artifact, and action step. Relay ingress rejects disallowed payloads before model invocation; Mac/browser agents attach signed, redacted evidence receipts; the pendant displays the active boundary and refuses to upload queued private audio until policy permits. args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can ask for help with genuinely sensitive material and receive useful results without having to trust that every component will remember a conversational promise not to upload it. args.effort: High: policy-token format and key management, relay enforcement at every route, local planner and browser evidence signing, encrypted pendant queue, audit UI, and negative tests proving forbidden routing is blocked.
args.risk: A policy bug could leak private content or make work silently unavailable. args.cost_impact: Minimal per-request compute and storage overhead; modest encrypted local ledger growth. No cloud model spend in strict local mode; engineering cost is substantial.
args.latency_impact: Adds tens of milliseconds for token checks and signing; local-only planning may be slower than realtime cloud responses but avoids network waits and retries.
args.security_impact: Strongly improves confidentiality and auditability, but introduces key-management and policy-configuration risk. The boundary must be enforced below the model prompt layer and audited independently.

On demand (and after firmware/relay changes), the pendant enters a 3-second local loopback test: it emits a marked playback sequence, captures the microphone return, and sends timestamped Opus frames plus clock/rate metadata. The ESP32 bridge reports I2S clock and underrun counters; the relay correlates input/output packet timestamps and verifies 24 kHz decoded output, resampling, jitter, loss, and half-duplex turn timing; the Mac agent stores a signed receipt and exposes a concise pass/fail report with the failing segment and recovery suggestion. During normal calls, retain only aggregate counters and raise a repair job when drift or repeated underruns cross thresholds, without retaining raw audio by default.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can know before a real conversation whether the pendant will actually capture and play intelligible 24 kHz audio, and gets a precise explanation when it will not. Silent clock drift, bridge underruns, and LTE timing failures become one actionable repair instead of a vague 'the audio sounded bad'.
args.effort: Medium-high: firmware test mode and counters, ESP32 bridge telemetry, relay correlation/validator, Mac receipt endpoint and a spoken/on-device result. Requires fixtures or a known acoustic loopback during manufacturing, plus field-test thresholds.
args.risk: A false failure could interrupt a conversation or prompt needless repair; keep certification manual/opt-in initially, never auto-reset during a call, and make the test abortible with the button. Acoustic environments can distort the loopback, so distinguish electrical/I2S loopback from room-acoustic confidence. Recovery is to fall back to the current 16 kHz uplink path and record diagnostics.
args.cost_impact: Negligible API cost: counters and one short test transcript/receipt; no raw audio retained unless explicitly enabled. Small firmware/bridge storage overhead; no new hardware required, though a factory jig microphone/speaker would improve calibration.
args.latency_impact: Adds about 3–5 seconds only when explicitly testing; normal calls add timestamp/counter handling with no model round trip.
args.security_impact: Raw test audio remains on-device/in transit only for the test and is discarded; receipts contain timing and quality metrics, not speech. Any upload of waveforms requires explicit consent.

transcript.text:
Recorded a new capability: **cross-surface privacy mode**.

The owner should be able to say, **“I’m in public—make this private,”** and have the pendant, relay, Mac, and browser simultaneously:

- mute or pause sensitive audio locally,
- stop screen capture and computer-use vision,
- hide authenticated browser tabs,
- cancel queued browser actions,
- suppress sensitive details from spoken responses,
- show which surfaces acknowledged privacy mode.

Returning to normal would require an explicit phrase or gesture, with an auditable receipt. This requires a signed shared privacy-state protocol, pendant firmware latch/status indication, Mac permission hooks, browser-extension masking, and relay-side sensitive-content enforcement.

args.body: Beyond existing durable jobs/receipts, propose a 'continuation lease': pendant utterance/button creates a signed intent capsule (goal, allowed surfaces, expiry, privacy class); relay persists it; Mac planner/browser execute only while lease valid. On link loss/restart, resume from last browser/Mac evidence checkpoint (not clicks), then pendant gives a terse spoken completion/failure. args.change: Introduce a cross-surface Continuation Lease protocol. The relay mints a short-lived, owner-confirmed lease containing a nonce, goal hash, permitted surfaces/domains/apps, allowed effect classes, expiry and approval requirements. Mac and browser workers must attach the lease nonce plus a semantic checkpoint ID and evidence hash to every result; after restart they can only reconcile from the latest checkpoint and must reject stale or replayed action IDs. args.why_useful_to_owner: A dropped link, sleeping Mac, or closed browser no longer loses a half-finished task or causes it to repeat an action. The owner can leave confidently, return to an exact explanation of what happened, and revoke authority from the pendant without opening the dashboard.

args.security_impact: Improves security by constraining authority and limiting relay data, but signing-key protection and nonce handling become critical. args.user_asks: “What was I in the middle of, and get me back to the exact place?”
args.why_useful: The owner often abandons a thought when a meeting, commute, or interruption arrives. Today the Mac, private browser, relay history, and pendant conversation do not form a single recoverable thread; the owner must search tabs and memory manually. This would reconstruct the unfinished intent, distinguish completed from merely viewed work, reopen the right private tabs/files, and offer the next safe step without pretending that an observed page means an action was completed.
surfaces: pendant: owner asks naturally and receives a short spoken reconstruction with confidence and one suggested next step
relay: correlates recent voice intents, job events, Mac checkpoints, and browser evidence into a privacy-scoped activity thread while the Mac may be asleep
mac-planner: inspects local windows/files/jobs and computes the unfinished-work hypothesis, reopening only the selected workspace
browser-extension: reports authenticated tab identity, scroll/selection/form state, and evidence of unsaved or unsubmitted work without sending contents to the relay
dashboard: displays a timeline with evidence, uncertainty, and explicit actions to reopen, discard, or continue
args.model_tier: Cheap background summarizer and deterministic event correlation for the initial reconstruction; a stronger planner only when multiple competing threads need judgment; realtime model only for the pendant exchange.
args.latency_budget: Spoken answer in 3 seconds for a recent thread; up to 15 seconds for cross-surface reconciliation. Never block on a remote browser if a locally evidenced partial answer can be spoken first.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.005–$0.04 per reconstruction; event correlation and local metadata dominate, with model tokens reserved for ambiguous threads. Do not upload full page bodies or audio by default.
args.security_concerns: Private browser contents, clipboard, microphone audio, and window titles can reveal sensitive work. Keep raw evidence on the Mac/browser, send relay only encrypted references, hashes, and minimal summaries, honor per-domain exclusion rules, and require confirmation before reopening a sensitive tab or restoring unsaved form data. Mark hypotheses as uncertain rather than claiming completion.

args.change: Add a provenance-first Activity Thread ledger shared by pendant, relay, Mac, and browser. Each event records thread candidate, source surface, local timestamp/monotonic sequence, evidence kind (voice intent, window/file focus, tab/form state, job result), sensitivity class, and expiry. A correlator periodically emits hypotheses with confidence and explicit gaps; it never upgrades 'viewed' or 'typed' into 'sent' or 'done'. Raw private payloads stay at their source, while the relay stores only encrypted references and minimal redacted summaries. The Mac and browser can consume a selected thread to restore a workspace non-destructively.
args.why_useful_to_owner: After an interruption, the owner can recover the exact unfinished thought instead of hunting through tabs and files or accidentally repeating a completed action. The system can say what it knows, what it only suspects, and put the owner back at the right place safely.
args.effort: High: event contracts and retention policy, Mac observer/checkpoint exporter, browser bridge state capture, relay correlation and encrypted reference store, dashboard timeline, pendant intent routing, and end-to-end privacy tests.
args.risk: Over-correlation could join unrelated sensitive work, and restoring stale editor or form state could lose changes. Mitigate with per-app/domain opt-in, short TTLs, cryptographic event IDs, confidence thresholds, read-only preview first, and explicit confirmation before reopening or restoring unsaved state. If any source is unavailable, show a partial timeline rather than infer.
args.cost_impact: Small durable metadata footprint; model cost roughly $0.005–$0.04 per reconstruction, dominated by ambiguous summarization. Raw content remains local, reducing relay storage and token cost.
args.latency_impact: Recent local recovery can be under 3 seconds; cross-surface correlation up to 15 seconds. Event append is asynchronous and should not affect voice latency.
args.security_impact: Adds a sensitive activity ledger, so encryption, domain/app exclusion, local deletion, and owner-visible retention controls are mandatory. Relay must not receive raw private page text, clipboard contents, or microphone recordings by default.

args.user_asks: “Keep track of the promises and follow-ups I make out loud. If I said I’d send, buy, schedule, or check something, watch the relevant logged-in pages and my Mac for evidence, then remind me only when it is still unresolved—and let me mark it done by voice.”
args.why_useful: A wearable hears commitments at the moment they happen, while the browser and Mac can verify whether they were actually completed. This closes the gap between a reminder list and reality, without flooding the owner with every note or unchanged page.
args.model_tier: Background extraction/classification uses a cheaper model; realtime is used only for the brief spoken confirmation and an on-demand status question. Browser/Mac evidence matching runs asynchronously.
args.latency_budget: Acknowledge capture on the pendant in under 1 second; create a tracked promise within 30 seconds; evidence checks run on their configured cadence (default hourly during waking hours), with urgent matches pushed within 2 minutes.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.01–$0.05 per captured commitment depending on transcript length and evidence checks; the dominant cost is authenticated page extraction, not the short classification call. Most checks should be skipped using change fingerprints.
args.security_concerns: Commitments and evidence may include private mail, calendar, purchases, or work pages. Store only a redacted commitment plus provenance and short-lived hashes by default; never read unrelated tabs, send messages, buy, or submit forms automatically. Voice “mark done” is reversible; any resulting external action requires the existing confirmation policy.
missing: A durable promise entity with lifecycle (open, snoozed, done, cancelled), confidence, due-window, and provenance linking an utterance to browser/Mac evidence
A cross-surface evidence matcher that can inspect only explicitly bound tabs/apps and distinguish completion from a merely similar page
A quiet-hours/escalation policy and pendant voice commands for snooze, status, and mark-done
A compact owner-facing promise queue and audit trail in the dashboard

result.note: Noted. Keep going — propose others, including ones that need capabilities that do not exist yet.

args.change: Add a cross-surface commitment/evidence ledger: each captured promise gets a compact typed record (utterance time, normalized intent, due window, sensitivity, allowed surfaces, confidence, and expiry). Browser and Mac workers append signed evidence observations with URL/app provenance, timestamp, semantic fingerprint, and match confidence; a relay reducer advances the lifecycle idempotently and emits one receipt or escalation. Keep raw audio and page text out of the ledger unless explicitly pinned.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can ask “what am I still supposed to do?” and get an honest answer grounded in what actually happened, rather than a stale reminder list. If a Mac or browser disconnects, the commitment remains intact and resumes without duplicate reminders.
args.effort: Medium-high: schema and reducer, authenticated provenance envelopes, extraction/matching worker, scheduler integration, dashboard queue, and pendant commands; build on existing job receipts and browser session affinity rather than replacing them.
args.risk: False matches could mark a promise complete or expose sensitive context. Require high confidence or explicit voice confirmation for completion, show source evidence, retain an undo transition, and expire unmatched observations. If the ledger is unavailable, keep a local encrypted capture and replay idempotently when relay returns.
args.cost_impact: Small durable storage and queue overhead; approximately one cheap classification call per commitment and incremental extraction only when a bound page changes. No realtime-model cost for background checks.
args.latency_impact: Voice capture acknowledgement stays sub-second; lifecycle updates are eventual (seconds to minutes) and should not block conversation. Dashboard status can be stale with an explicit freshness timestamp.
args.security_impact: Least-privilege per commitment (specific tab/app bindings), redacted fields and short retention, encrypted transport/storage, and no automatic external side effects. Provenance lets the owner inspect exactly why an item was considered done.
depends_on: A durable browser job runner with tab/session affinity and typed results
A typed context projection with sensitivity and TTL
An offline pendant capture spool and delivery receipt
A durable scheduler/queue with idempotency keys

result.note: Noted. Keep going, including layers you have not touched yet.
